Where it began

Mark Anthony Taylor was born on 27 October 1964 in Leeton, New South Wales, and grew up in Wagga Wagga after the family moved there when he was eight. He enjoyed rugby, but cricket came first, and his first batting lessons came in the garage at home, against cork balls.

He made his first hundred at 13 for the Lake Albert club in Wagga, then moved with the family to Sydney's north shore and joined Northern District. He played youth internationals alongside the Waugh twins, took a surveying degree at the University of New South Wales, and first opened for New South Wales in 1985.

The player

Few Test careers have started like his. After a quiet debut early in 1989, he went to England for that year's Ashes and made 839 runs in six Tests, with a hundred at Headingley in his first Test of the tour and 219 at Trent Bridge, where he and Geoff Marsh batted through an entire day. By the end of 1989 he had become the first man to pass a thousand Test runs in the calendar year of his debut, and Wisden named him one of its Cricketers of the Year.

In 104 Tests up to 1999 he scored 7,525 runs at 43.50, with 19 hundreds and 40 fifties.

What made him special

At first slip he caught nearly everything. He finished with 157 Test catches, at the time more than anyone had ever taken. As captain from 1994 to 1999 he was bold and positive, cheerful in a way his team-mates noticed, and keen to cut down sledging. Of his 50 Tests in charge, Australia won 26 and lost 13, and in 1995 his side took a series in the Caribbean, something no Australian team had managed for 22 years.

At Peshawar in 1998 he batted for two days to make 334 not out, equalling Don Bradman's Australian record. Everyone expected him to go on the next morning. Instead he declared, sharing the record with Bradman and putting the team first. One-day cricket suited him less well than the Test game, and in 1997 he went through a lean spell with the bat, but he answered it with a hundred in the first Test of that summer's Ashes.

Away from the middle

He was Australian of the Year in 1999, and in 2003 he became an Officer of the Order of Australia. He went into the Sport Australia Hall of Fame and, in 2011, Cricket Australia's Hall of Fame. Afterwards he became a long-serving commentator with Channel Nine and a director of Cricket Australia. In 2011 Northern District renamed their home ground Mark Taylor Oval.

And finally

He shares a curious record with Ian Healy: they are the only two men to have been run out in each innings of the same Test, and on two different occasions. For one of the game's great catchers, the running between the wickets was a gentle reminder that nobody is perfect.
